label: Curvature Meets Group Theory
notes: Open by framing the chapter as a dictionary. A group that acts properly and cocompactly by isometries on a CAT(0) space inherits a usable geometry, and that geometry forces algebraic facts. Stress that the action, not an abstract presentation, is what gives us leverage over otherwise hard group-theoretic questions.

label: CAT(0) Groups
notes: Define a CAT(0) group precisely: it acts properly, cocompactly, by isometries on a complete CAT(0) space. By the Svarc-Milnor lemma such a group is finitely generated and quasi-isometric to the space. Emphasize that cocompactness is what transfers convexity of the metric into combinatorial control of the Cayley graph.

label: The Translation Dictionary
notes: Walk the dictionary row by row. Cocompact action corresponds to a quasi-isometry, flats correspond to abelian subgroups, convexity corresponds to the absence of distortion. The point is methodological: prove a geometric statement about the space, then read off the algebraic consequence for the group without touching a presentation.

label: Semisimple Isometries and Translation
notes: Recall the trichotomy of isometries and focus on hyperbolic ones with positive translation length achieved on an axis. In a CAT(0) group every infinite-order element acts as a semisimple isometry, so it has an axis. This is the geometric engine behind the Flat Torus theorem on the next slide.

label: Flat Torus Theorem
notes: State the Flat Torus theorem: a free abelian subgroup of rank n stabilizes an isometrically embedded flat, a copy of Euclidean n-space, and the quotient contains a flat n-torus. Make the slogan explicit: abelian subgroups are exactly flats. Rank of the abelian subgroup equals dimension of the flat it preserves.

label: Solvable Subgroup Theorem
notes: State that every solvable subgroup of a CAT(0) group is virtually abelian, in fact finitely generated and virtually free abelian when the action is cocompact. Contrast with general groups, where solvable subgroups are wild. Non-positive curvature collapses solvability down to flat geometry, which is the recurring moral of the chapter.

label: Centralizers and Splitting
notes: Explain how axes organize centralizers. The centralizer of a hyperbolic isometry splits as a product of a line with a complementary space, so the centralizer of an infinite-order element virtually splits with a central Z factor. This product structure is the tool that proves the Flat Torus and Solvable Subgroup theorems.

label: A Tits Alternative Flavor
notes: Describe the dichotomy: a subgroup of a CAT(0) group is either virtually abelian or contains a rank-one element giving free, ping-pong dynamics on the boundary. It is not the full Tits alternative in general, but for many CAT(0) groups one gets the clean split between flat behavior and free, hyperbolic-like behavior.

label: Dehn Functions and van Kampen Diagrams
notes: Define the Dehn or isoperimetric function as the maximal area needed to fill a null-homotopic loop of given length by a van Kampen diagram. Emphasize the picture: a loop in the Cayley two-complex bounds a disc tiled by relator cells, and area counts those cells. The growth rate of this function is a quasi-isometry invariant.

label: Quadratic Filling for CAT(0)
notes: State the key inequality: CAT(0) groups satisfy a quadratic isoperimetric inequality, area bounded by a constant times length squared. Convexity lets you cone the loop to a basepoint and bound the swept area. Contrast with hyperbolic groups, which improve this to a linear bound, the sharper extreme of non-positive curvature.

label: Distortion and Quasi-convex Subgroups
notes: Define subgroup distortion comparing the intrinsic and ambient word metrics. An undistorted, quasi-convex subgroup embeds without stretching, like a flat or a convex core. Distorted subgroups, such as fibers in certain mapping tori, show that not every subgroup of a non-positively curved group is itself well behaved.

label: Decision Problems and the CAT(0) vs Hyperbolic Divide
notes: Close with algorithms. CAT(0) and biautomatic structures make the word problem solvable with a quadratic bound; biautomaticity also yields the conjugacy problem in good cases. Summarize the divide: hyperbolic groups are the linear, strongly contracting extreme, CAT(0) groups the quadratic, flat-tolerant world that still keeps decision problems tractable.
